meta.description: Non-native species that threaten the Everglades and South Florida.

reporting.note: Florida's invasive species reporting hotline and app.

pythons.note: Carried over from the original homepage copy. Confirm against current FWC or SFWMD python program totals before publishing.

harm_types.title: They eat native wildlife
harm_types.description: Predators with no natural enemies here can wipe out prey that never evolved defenses against them, including eggs, young animals, and whole populations.

harm_types.title: They crowd out native species
harm_types.description: Invaders compete with native plants and animals for food, nesting space, and sunlight, and they often win because nothing here keeps them in check.

harm_types.title: They change the habitat
harm_types.description: Dense thickets and mats replace open marsh and forest, changing what lives there. Native animals that depend on the original habitat lose food and shelter.

harm_types.title: They poison or injure
harm_types.description: Some invaders carry toxins, venom, or irritating sap that can harm pets, wildlife, and people who come into contact with them.

harm_types.title: They change how fire behaves
harm_types.description: Many Everglades habitats burn naturally. Some invasive plants burn hotter, climb into treetops, or spread after fire, which turns a normal burn into a damaging one.

harm_types.title: They damage property
harm_types.description: Burrowing animals undermine seawalls and canal banks, and small animals that hide in electrical equipment can cause outages and costly repairs.

species.summary: A giant constrictor that has devastated native mammal populations in the Everglades.
species.description: Burmese pythons became established in the Everglades after escaping or being released from the pet trade. They are top predators with few natural enemies here and can grow well over 15 feet long.
impact: Research has documented severe declines in raccoons, opossums, bobcats, and marsh rabbits in areas with pythons
Preys on wading birds and other native wildlife
Competes with native predators such as alligators and native snakes
identification_tips: Large snake with irregular dark brown blotches on a tan background
Blotches are outlined in a lighter color, like puzzle pieces
Dark arrowhead-shaped mark on top of the head
native_lookalikes: Native rat snakes and watersnakes are far smaller and more slender
what_to_do: Do not approach or handle it
Take a photo from a safe distance and note the location
Report it through the IveGot1 app or the hotline
Never release a pet; use FWC's Exotic Pet Amnesty Program instead

species.summary: A large lizard that damages seawalls and landscaping and eats native plants.
species.description: Green iguanas are common in canals and yards across South Florida. Cold snaps can stun them so they fall from trees, but populations quickly rebound.
impact: Burrows undermine seawalls, canal banks, and sidewalks
Feeds on native plants, including some that rare butterflies depend on
Droppings can foul docks, pools, and water
identification_tips: Green to gray-brown with a spiny crest down the back
Large, round scale below the ear
Banded tail; adults can reach about 5 feet
native_lookalikes: The native green anole is only a few inches long
what_to_do: Do not feed iguanas
Ask a licensed wildlife trapper for help with nuisance animals
Report iguanas in protected natural areas
Never release a pet iguana

species.origin: Cuba, the Bahamas, and the Cayman Islands
species.summary: A big, hungry tree frog that eats native frogs.
species.description: Cuban tree frogs are common around South Florida homes, where they hide in pipes, mailboxes, and light fixtures. They are larger than any native tree frog in Florida.
impact: Eats native tree frogs and their tadpoles
Skin secretions can irritate eyes and noses
Can short out electrical equipment
identification_tips: Up to about 5 inches long, much bigger than native tree frogs
Warty-looking skin and very large toe pads
Color varies from white to green to gray or brown
what_to_do: Wear gloves and wash your hands after handling any frog
Do not relocate non-native frogs to another area
Ask UF/IFAS Extension about humane removal in your yard

species.summary: A big omnivorous lizard that raids the nests of native wildlife.
species.description: Tegus have established breeding populations in parts of South Florida, including Miami-Dade County. They eat almost anything, including eggs, and dig burrows to shelter in.
impact: Eats eggs of ground-nesting birds, crocodilians, and turtles
Preys on small native animals
Populations can grow quickly once established
identification_tips: Adults reach 3 to 4 feet with black and white bands
Beaded-looking scales
Young tegus can have bright green heads and backs
native_lookalikes: Native racerunners are small, slender, and striped
what_to_do: Do not handle it; tegus can bite hard
Take a photo and report it through IveGot1
Never release a pet tegu

species.summary: A huge toad whose toxin can seriously sicken or kill dogs and cats.
species.description: Cane toads are found in South Florida neighborhoods, especially near lights that attract insects and around outdoor pet food. They produce a milky toxin from glands behind the eyes.
impact: Toxin can poison dogs and cats that mouth or lick them
Competes with native amphibians for food
Eats native insects and small animals
identification_tips: Large, up to 6 inches or more
Bony ridges above the eyes running down the snout
Large, triangular glands behind each eye
native_lookalikes: Southern toad (smaller, with two bony knobs between the eyes)
what_to_do: Keep pets away and bring pet food inside at night
If a pet mouths a toad, rinse its mouth with water and call a vet or animal poison control right away
Wear gloves if you handle one and wash your hands

species.summary: A venomous reef fish that eats native young fish faster than they can recover.
species.description: Lionfish are established across Florida's coastal waters, including reefs off South Florida. They reproduce year-round and have few natural predators here.
impact: Eats large numbers of young native reef fish
Competes with native predators such as snappers and groupers
Spines can deliver a painful sting
identification_tips: Red-brown and white stripes
Long, fan-like fins
Venomous spines along the back
native_lookalikes: Native scorpionfishes have shorter fins and are less showy
what_to_do: Do not touch it; the spines are venomous
If stung, soak the area in hot (not scalding) water and get medical care
Divers can report sightings through the Reef Environmental Education Foundation (REEF)

species.summary: A fast-spreading shrub that forms dense thickets and shades out native plants.
species.description: Brazilian pepper was brought to Florida as an ornamental and now grows across disturbed land, canal banks, and natural areas. Birds spread its berries widely.
impact: Forms dense thickets that crowd out native plants
Changes habitat for native wildlife
Sap can cause skin reactions in sensitive people
identification_tips: Shiny compound leaves with several leaflets
Bright red berries in clusters in fall and winter
Sometimes sold as "Florida holly"
what_to_do: Do not plant it
Wear gloves and long sleeves when removing seedlings
Put berries in the trash, not the compost
Hire a licensed professional for large trees

species.origin: Australia, Papua New Guinea, and New Caledonia
species.summary: An Australian tree that replaced open sawgrass marsh with dense forest.
species.description: Melaleuca was planted in South Florida in the early 1900s in hopes of drying wetlands. It spread widely through the Everglades, though biological control insects have helped slow it.
impact: Forms dense stands that displace sawgrass marsh and wet prairie
Releases large amounts of seed after fire or damage
Reduces habitat for native wildlife
identification_tips: Thick, papery white bark that peels off in layers
Narrow, leathery, pointed leaves that smell spicy when crushed
Bottlebrush-like white flower spikes
native_lookalikes: Ornamental bottlebrush (Callistemon) is a related garden plant
what_to_do: Do not plant it
Report dense stands in natural areas to the land manager
Use licensed professionals to remove trees safely

species.summary: A climbing fern that smothers tree islands and carries fire into the treetops.
species.description: Old World climbing fern grows into dense mats that climb into shrubs and trees. It is one of the most damaging invaders of Everglades tree islands and other wetland forests.
impact: Smothers native plants under thick mats
Acts as a ladder that carries fire into tree canopies
Spreads by tiny wind-blown spores
identification_tips: Wiry, twining stems that climb up other plants
Delicate, bright-green, finely divided leaflets
Often found in dense tangles on trees and shrubs
native_lookalikes: Native leather fern grows upright and does not climb
what_to_do: Do not move or dump yard waste containing fern into natural areas
Report infestations in natural areas to the land manager
Clean boots and gear after visiting infested areas

species.summary: A large African lizard that raids the nests of protected native animals.
species.description: Nile monitors are large, semi-aquatic lizards that reached Florida through the pet trade, as escaped or released pets. Breeding populations now live in parts of Palm Beach and Lee counties. Florida added the species to its Prohibited species list in 2021, so it is illegal to buy or keep one as a pet.
impact: Eats almost anything it can overpower, including fish, birds, eggs, and small animals
Raids nests of protected animals such as gopher tortoises, burrowing owls, and the American crocodile
Spreads along canals and waterways, which can carry it into new areas
identification_tips: Large lizard that commonly reaches about 5 feet and can grow longer than 6 feet
Olive, brown, or gray body with yellow-green bands or spots, and a banded tail
Long neck, strong claws, and a forked tongue that flicks in and out
Often seen near canals and the edges of water
native_lookalikes: Florida's native lizards, such as anoles and skinks, are far smaller
what_to_do: Do not approach or try to capture it; it can be very defensive when cornered
Take a photo from a safe distance and note the location
Report it through the IveGot1 app or the hotline
Never release a pet; use FWC's Exotic Pet Amnesty Program instead
